stimulus.title: Why Do Leaves Change Colour?
stimulus.body: Every autumn, forests across southern Australia put on a quiet but spectacular display as certain deciduous trees shift from green to gold, orange and deep red. The transformation is not caused by cooling temperatures alone, but by a gradual reduction in daylight hours, which signals to the tree that winter is approaching. Throughout spring and summer, leaves are dominated by chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight and gives leaves their familiar green colour. As daylight shortens, trees begin to reabsorb chlorophyll from their leaves, effectively recycling a valuable resource before the leaves are shed. Once the green pigment fades, other pigments that were present all along, but masked by the abundant chlorophyll, finally become visible. Some trees also produce brand new red pigments at this time, possibly as a defence against sunlight damage while the tree withdraws its remaining nutrients.

options.text: Because the tree is most exposed to potential sunlight damage while it is vulnerable, withdrawing its remaining nutrients.
Because red pigment is only visible to humans once the weather turns cold.
Because chlorophyll production increases during this period, requiring extra protection.
Because the tree is attracting insects to help spread its seeds before winter.

items.explanation: The passage links the new red pigment directly to a protective purpose, 'a defence against sunlight damage while the tree withdraws its remaining nutrients.' This timing detail shows the protection is needed precisely because the tree is in a vulnerable state while withdrawing those nutrients during leaf shedding, not during summer.

options.text: To take a substance back into the plant after it had been held elsewhere in the leaf.

items.prompt: Based on the whole passage, which statement best describes how Nadia most likely felt as the bee sat on her sleeve, even though the text never states her feelings directly at that moment?

stimulus.title: The Beekeeper's Warning
stimulus.body: Nadia had visited her grandfather's orchard every summer since she could walk, but she had never been allowed near the beehives until this year. 'Bees are not our enemies,' her grandfather said, tightening the strap on her borrowed veil, 'but they are diplomats, not pushovers. Move like a shadow, and they will forgive almost anything.' Nadia laughed nervously, though her stomach had turned into a nest of hornets itself. As they approached the first hive, she noticed her grandfather's steps slow to an almost theatrical crawl, his breathing low and even. A single bee landed on her sleeve and simply sat there, as if deciding whether she was worth the trouble of a sting. Nadia held perfectly still, remembering his warning, and after a long moment the bee lifted off and drifted back towards the hive entrance without incident.

options.text: She felt tense and cautious, but was consciously fighting the urge to move.
She felt completely relaxed, since her grandfather's advice had already erased all her fear.
She felt bored, since she had expected something more exciting to happen with the bees.
She felt angry at her grandfather for putting her in a risky situation.

items.explanation: Earlier in the passage, Nadia's stomach is described as being like 'a nest of hornets,' showing she was nervous even while laughing on the surface. This nervousness does not disappear simply because her grandfather gave her advice; it is only managed, not erased. When the bee lands, the text says she 'held perfectly still, remembering his warning,' which implies a deliberate, conscious effort to stay calm rather than genuine relaxation. Together, these details point to a tense-but-controlled state, not boredom, anger, or true relaxation.

items.prompt: Considering the passage as a whole, how does Tomas's emotional state most likely shift between the moment he starts sprinting and the moment he watches the pier shrink into the distance?

stimulus.title: The Last Ferry
stimulus.body: Tomas sprinted down the pier, his backpack thumping against his spine like an impatient drum. The ferry's horn had already sounded twice, and its gangway was folding upward with the slow, deliberate finality of a closing book. 'Wait!' he shouted, though his voice was swallowed by the wind rolling off the harbour. A deckhand glanced up, hesitated, then waved sharply at the captain. The gangway paused, hovering halfway, before creaking back down just long enough for Tomas to leap aboard, stumbling onto the deck as the ferry's engines rumbled to life beneath his feet. He caught his breath against the railing, watching the pier and its silent, indifferent clock tower shrink slowly into the grey afternoon.

options.text: From urgent panic to relieved exhaustion, once he is safely aboard.
From calm confidence to sudden terror, once the ferry begins moving.
From boredom to excitement, once he notices the clock tower.
From anger at the deckhand to gratitude towards the captain.

items.explanation: Tomas is shown sprinting and shouting urgently at the start, clearly desperate and panicked about catching the ferry. That urgency could easily continue if he were still worried about something once aboard. Instead, by the end, he is described catching his breath against the railing and watching the pier 'shrink slowly,' a much calmer image than the frantic sprint. This shift suggests relief now that the danger of missing the ferry has passed, rather than any of the other emotional changes listed.

stimulus.title: The New Coach
stimulus.body: When Priya heard that Mr Okafor was taking over the under-12s football team, she groaned loudly enough for her older brother to hear from the next room. The old coach had let the team choose their own drills and finish training whenever they felt tired. On the first afternoon, Mr Okafor lined everyone up along the halfway line and simply said, 'We're going to run before we kick a single ball.' Priya rolled her eyes, certain the season was about to become miserable. Three weeks later, though, she found herself arriving fifteen minutes early to training, lacing up her boots before anyone else. Her passes were sharper, her legs no longer burned after ten minutes, and for the first time she could outrun the girl who had always beaten her to the ball.

options.text: A stricter training approach can lead to real, unexpected improvement, even when it is unwelcome at first.
Football teams should always let players choose their own drills.
Priya's brother plays an important role in her football career.
Running is the only skill that matters in football.

items.explanation: The passage traces Priya's journey from dreading Mr Okafor's strict training to genuinely benefiting from it. This overall arc, not any single detail like her brother or the running drills alone, is what the passage is really about.

items.prompt: According to the text, what is the main signal that tells a tree it is time to begin changing its leaf colour?

stimulus.title: Why Do Leaves Change Colour?
stimulus.body: Every autumn, forests across southern Australia put on a quiet but spectacular display as certain deciduous trees shift from green to gold, orange and deep red. The transformation is not caused by cooling temperatures alone, but by a gradual reduction in daylight hours, which signals to the tree that winter is approaching. Throughout spring and summer, leaves are dominated by chlorophyll, the pigment that captures sunlight and gives leaves their familiar green colour. As daylight shortens, trees begin to reabsorb chlorophyll from their leaves, effectively recycling a valuable resource before the leaves are shed. Once the green pigment fades, other pigments that were present all along, but masked by the abundant chlorophyll, finally become visible. Some trees also produce brand new red pigments at this time, possibly as a defence against sunlight damage while the tree withdraws its remaining nutrients.

options.text: A gradual reduction in the number of daylight hours.
A sudden drop in temperature overnight.
The complete disappearance of chlorophyll from the leaf.
The production of new red pigments in the leaves.

items.explanation: The text states the transformation 'is not caused by cooling temperatures alone, but by a gradual reduction in daylight hours, which signals to the tree that winter is approaching.' This identifies shortening daylight, not temperature or the other listed effects, as the main trigger.

options.text: Careful negotiators who can be reasonable, but should not be treated carelessly.
Government officials who work in a real embassy.

items.explanation: Calling bees 'diplomats, not pushovers' is a metaphor comparing them to careful negotiators: reasonable if treated respectfully, but not creatures to be treated carelessly. It is not a literal claim about government work, since bees clearly cannot hold an official diplomatic position. The phrase also rules out the idea of bees being weak or unreactive, since a 'pushover' is exactly that kind of easily-overcome creature, and the grandfather is denying that description. Equally, calling them diplomats rather than simply dangerous suggests they are not aggressive without reason, but capable of being reasoned with under the right conditions.
